report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Approach anxiety (AA) describes a fear or intense nervousness about approaching or initiating social and especially dating interactions, where approach and avoidance goals collide.

We review literature on AA in the context of human dating behavior to (a) evaluate the scientific status of AA as a distinct psychological concept and construct and (b) identify key associations with and causes of AA.

Our scoping review identified zero studies of AA specifically, despite the widespread recognition of AA in popular media and self-help platforms, although we identified 83 studies of psychological dynamics during the initial phase of social interaction.
Academic literature seems to ignore AA despite the many young men who say AA is a major problem.

We provide a AA construct clarification and evidence integration of studies of youth social interaction dynamics which describe social or dating anxiety, fear of rejection, or heterosocial competence.
AA describes a complex interplay of sex differences, attachment styles, cultural expectations, and individual psychological factors.

We present a Multilevel Courtship Inhibition Framework (MCIF) of AA that connects social skill deficits and psychological challenges with potential evolutionary, sociocultural, and psychological underpinnings, to help catalyze academic AA research.

Introduction "Dating" is a social activity where two humans spend time together to assess their mutual compatibility ("go out"), typically with the expectation or hope to develop a romantic (or potentially sexual) relationship, with dating as an active verb that seeks an outcome.
Modern dating patterns emerged in America and expanded relationship possibilities beyond traditional social circles and courtship norms and marriage (Waller, 1937; Fass, 1977).

text.text: Evidently there is no formal academic definition of "approach anxiety" or associated phenomena, despite being used frequently online, as outlined in this review.

Below we peruse and synthesize the literature on AA in men in social dating contexts to identify the key themes and gaps in AA research and the implications of AA focusing on four questions: namely, what (1) is the current state of research on "approach anxiety" in social dating among men; (2) which psychological factors associated with AA in social dating; (3) how is AA conceptualized/measured in studies of social dating contexts; and (4) what are the gaps in the existing literature on AA in men?

Our scoping review followed a systematic search strategy to identified articles across eight different electronic databases: Smartcat (university platform), PsycINFO (mainly for psychology related subjects), SociNDEX (social sciences), MEDLINE (medical), Web of Science (science), Scopus (science), PubMed (medical), and Google Scholar.

People who experience difficulties initiating contact in social or romantic settings can feel (extremely) nervous, fearful, insecure and/or in discomfort in social situations, which is called social anxiety and key to many anxiety symptoms and disorders.

Many specific anxieties have been distinguished, such as dating anxiety when interacting with potential romantic partners, or heterosocial anxiety in social situations with members of the opposite sex, which may share underlying psychological and biological machinery with AA, such as approach inhibitions.
Below we now dissect four of these categories in detail.
Subsequently, we discuss the role of rejection in relationship initiation, and how AA relates to attachment.

Approach anxiety (AA) is a concept that gained prominence in dating and coaching circles and features widely across self-help platforms and media.

We critically examined the scientific foundation of the AA construct and perused the peer-reviewed academic literature to conclude that the AA concept has been largely absent from the peer-reviewed scholarship.
This lack of AA research was striking given the prevalence of the AA concept in popular discourse, in particular around male-initiated romantic interactions.

We explored whether AA is an academically unrecognized concept (phenomenon) that is still largely restricted to popular culture, or whether AA was studied as a neighbouring concept with specific terminology (e.g., dating anxiety).

Below we discuss whether AA demands different terminology, and synthesize our main findings into a Multilevel Courtship Inhibition Framework (MCIF) of AA and outline how this MCIF-AA model spurs novel hypotheses and research avenues.
AA appears to have originated from the American pickup artist (PUA) community, which centers on strategies for attracting romantic or sexual partners.

While the precise origin of the term is difficult to determine, Neil Strauss's The Game (2005) is among the earliest widely recognized texts to describe the fear of approaching women (to denote acute anxiety and behavioral inhibition that arises immediately before initiating an interaction).

text.text: Limited empirical research has examined the extent to which American dating culture, including its terminology, influences native and global perspectives on romantic behavior.

It is therefore plausible that the absence of AA in scientific literature stems from its potentially artificial status, shaped by the commercial interests of dating industries, linguistic limitations, or sociocultural dynamics specific to the United States (Bachaud et al., 2025).

text.text: We reviewed existing interdisciplinary knowledge to critically evaluate the AA construct's conceptual foundations and overlap with heterosocial anxiety, dating anxiety, heterosexual-social anxiety, dating inhibitions, social interaction anxiety, and fear of negative evaluation in dating contexts.
We provide a foundation for a systematic inquiry into the dynamics of dating initiation, which has received comparatively little attention (despite dating being heavily researched).
The complexity of the initial stages stands out as a key area of inquiry.

Due to the lack of direct literature on AA, we identified 29 alternative terms with potential relevance to men's fear of initiating relationships, as outlined in Figure 1, which provides a conceptual map of these terms associated with AA and initial encounters, and can be strengthened and refined in future research.

text.text: We distinguish between direct effects on AA (represented by solid lines) and indirect effects (dashed lines) to underscore the complexity of the relationships among interpersonal competence, emotional responses, and avoidance behaviors.
These pathways highlight the interplay between skills deficits, anxiety, and maladaptive coping strategies, which emphasizes the multifaceted nature of AA anxiety in social and romantic contexts.
At the center of the model is AA, potentially linked to interpersonal performance represented on the left, encompassing factors such as social skills and competence.

Certain concepts play a more critical role than others in understanding AA; social competence has been extensively studied (Scott, 2006), for example, with findings highlighting that heterosocial skills significantly affect how men approach women and how secure they feel in doing so (Kelly, 1982; Grover et al., 2005).

text.text: Also, low interpersonal competence (low grasp on social cues and norms, see Twentyman, 1981) is associated with dating anxiety (Adamczyk and Segrin, 2016), which underscores that social skills are key to AA, although research needs to confirm this relationship, especially over adolescence (Connolly et al., 2000; Nangle & Hansen, 1998), when heterosocial incompetence seems directly connected to AA.

text.text: Psychological contributors to AA include anxiety (anticipatory social anxiety, dating anxiety, and specific anxiety), and future work may explore these associations in detail, and fear of rejection and fear of social interaction (or social phobia), often discussed in terms of attachment styles (i.e.
"mechanisms" that [can] exert in/direct effects on AA).
The following paragraphs will try to explain the potentially individual contributions to AA.
Anxiety.
AA is closely tied to the broader construct of anxiety, as men with AA are thought to exhibit a generalized fear of initiating interactions with women.

AA can be distinguished from general dating anxiety because AA is more prevalent, and AA seems to impose specific but substantial social limitations, which partly overlap with the discourse on shyness (e.g., Scott, 2006; also Larsen et al., 2025).

text.text: Our review indicates that between 30% and 60% of college students experience significant anxiety or shyness in opposite-sex interactions, with men disproportionately affected, particularly in the context of initiating romantic approaches (McNamara & Grossman, 1991; Arkowitz et al., 1978; Grover, 2002).

text.text: Social anxiety research highlights specific difficulties men face in social and romantic contexts and the role of avoidance learning (Hofmann & Hay, 2018).
text.formatted: Social anxiety research highlights specific difficulties men face in social and romantic contexts and the role of avoidance learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(Hofmann & Hay, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals with high social anxiety tend to avoid other-sex interactions, perform poorly in social situations, and report lower satisfaction in these interactions compared to those with lower anxiety levels (Dodge et al., 1987).
text.formatted: Individuals with high social anxiety tend to avoid other-sex interactions, perform poorly in social situations, and report lower satisfaction in these interactions compared to those with lower anxiety levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Dodge et al., 1987)</ref>.

text.text: For men, this avoidance behavior may stem from a combination of low self-perceived mate value and fear of rejection, leading them to favor interactions with individuals they perceive as less physically attractive (Wenzel, 2009; O'Neill, 2015).
text.formatted: For men, this avoidance behavior may stem from a combination of low self-perceived mate value and fear of rejection, leading them to favor interactions with individuals they perceive as less physically attractive <ref type="bibr" target="#b203">(Wenzel, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">O'Neill, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Socially anxious men often believe others are less likely to engage with them, which can reinforce a cycle of avoidance and missed opportunities to approach women.

Additionally, socially anxious men often struggle to form same-sex friendships and broader social networks (Barnett et al., 2020; Himadi et al., 1980), depriving them of opportunities to build self-esteem and practice the interpersonal skills necessary for romantic contexts.
text.formatted: Additionally, socially anxious men often struggle to form same-sex friendships and broader social networks <ref type="bibr">(Barnett et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Himadi et al., 1980)</ref>, depriving them of opportunities to build self-esteem and practice the interpersonal skills necessary for romantic contexts.

text.text: The compounding effects of low self-perceived mate value, fear of rejection, and limited social competence, suggest that anxiety can be a significant obstacle for men in approaching women, and highlight the importance of addressing social anxiety within the framework of romantic relationship initiation.
Anxiety can become so intense that it physically inhibits the individual.

While research consistently finds that women report higher levels of anxiety than men (Bourdon et al., 1988; Costello et al., 2004; Farhane-Medina et al., 2022), the nature of anxiety symptoms differs significantly between the sexes.

text.text: Men often externalize anxiety through physical symptoms, such as headaches, trembling, and a sensation of losing control (Auerbach et al., 2012; Bender et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Men often externalize anxiety through physical symptoms, such as headaches, trembling, and a sensation of losing control <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Auerbach et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Bender et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This externalization can create a barrier to acknowledging or addressing anxiety's impact on interpersonal interactions, including approaching potential romantic partners.
Next to mental and physical origins, cultural and developmental factors tied to sex socialization may exacerbate AA struggles.

Men are often socialized to mask emotional vulnerabilities, which can limit their willingness to seek help or openly discuss anxieties related to dating and relationships (Craske, 2003; McLean et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Men are often socialized to mask emotional vulnerabilities, which can limit their willingness to seek help or openly discuss anxieties related to dating and relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Craske, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">McLean et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative studies further emphasize that men tend to perceive anxiety as an uncontrollable, externalized force, which could lead to a sense of helplessness in addressing the fear of initiating romantic interactions (Drioli-Phillips et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Qualitative studies further emphasize that men tend to perceive anxiety as an uncontrollable, externalized force, which could lead to a sense of helplessness in addressing the fear of initiating romantic interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Drioli-Phillips et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This perception may discourage them from developing the social skills needed to approach women confidently.
Returning to the initial question of whether AA is a genuine psychological construct or simply a form of anxiety, only future research can provide clarity and answer this uncertainty.
Fear.
AA does not have to manifest itself as severe anxiety, and can be understood as an immediate, situational fear response.

Research indicates that fear of rejection significantly impacts dating dynamics, with 76% of undergraduates reporting that it has prevented them from pursuing a romantic relationship at least once, and 54% stating it has completely deterred them (Vorauer & Ratner, 1996).
text.formatted: Research indicates that fear of rejection significantly impacts dating dynamics, with 76% of undergraduates reporting that it has prevented them from pursuing a romantic relationship at least once, and 54% stating it has completely deterred them <ref type="bibr" target="#b200">(Vorauer & Ratner, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Several theories can explain this relationship (Hoffman & Hay, 2018), such as the theory of belonging regulation, which builds on Baumeister and Leary's (1995) conceptualization of belonging as a fundamental human need, and identifies fear of rejection as a direct threat to social belonging.

text.text: Our review suggests a potential link between AA and fear of rejection and the need to further explore this relationship.
We therefore added a direct relationship between fear and AA to Figure 1, and an indirect path via the lack of social skills.

text.text: Phobia.
Social phobia might be the extreme form of men struggling to approach women.
Closely tied high communication apprehension is linked to lower social skills with the opposite sex, greater anxiety, and increased fear of social interactions.
Together, these factors often lead to avoidance in dating situations, especially when approaching women (Cox, 2009; Hoffman & Hay, 2018).
text.formatted: Together, these factors often lead to avoidance in dating situations, especially when approaching women <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Cox, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hoffman & Hay, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, individuals with high communication apprehension often perceive themselves as less physically attractive, further exacerbating their reluctance to initiate social interactions.
The reviewed literature on social phobia and its impact on dating remains limited and no studies specifically addressed AA.
Another potential factor to consider for inclusion in the model presented in Figure 1 is the possibility that a certain percentage of men may indeed develop something akin to AA.

text.text: Attachment theory is a well-established area of research with significant insights into dating dynamics; however, its application to the earliest stages of romantic initiation remains relatively underexplored.

Avoidant attachment is linked to lower desire for partners, making it harder for men with this trait to initiate romantic approaches, and leading them to seek less emotionally involved encounters (Blumenstock, 2023; Coffey et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Avoidant attachment is linked to lower desire for partners, making it harder for men with this trait to initiate romantic approaches, and leading them to seek less emotionally involved encounters <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Blumenstock, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Coffey et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Men with higher attachment anxiety experience fewer matches, likely due to lower popularity, while anxiety does not impact women's match success (McClure et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Men with higher attachment anxiety experience fewer matches, likely due to lower popularity, while anxiety does not impact women's match success <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">(McClure et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Societal norms, which position men as the primary initiators, exacerbate this pressure and anxiety.

Additionally, men who prefer women to take a more direct approach in dating tend to exhibit higher relationship anxiety, reflecting insecurities linked to their attachment style (Barhana, 2015). Contrarily, Guynn et al. (2008) found that securely attached men do not initiate romantic interactions at higher rates, as preoccupied individuals do.

(2008)</ref> found that securely attached men do not initiate romantic interactions at higher rates, as preoccupied individuals do.

text.text: Secure individuals, more comfortable being single, tend to refrain from initiating, and allow women to take the lead.
Replicating these studies is crucial to further explore these processes and in particularly men's responses when approached by women.

Reportedly securely attached individuals are less likely to experience AA (~40-60% of American population, Meng et al., 2015), and if AA proves to be closely tied to attachment styles, this could help researchers better understand AA.

text.text: If only a subset of men experience AA the "anxiety" may be a specific response influenced by individual personality traits, such as shyness (Scott, 2006; Larsen et al., 2025).

text.text: Shyness can either strengthen or limit interpersonal abilities (Davis & Buss, 2012; Baardstu et al., 2023), and function as a mediator of interpersonal performance, or directly affect AA.

text.text: Shyness has been shown to negatively impact interpersonal competence, complicating efforts to initiate conversations or express emotions effectively (Bruch, 1998; Larsen et al., 2025).

text.text: These difficulties can escalate anxiety in social contexts, making the act of approaching women more daunting.
Shy individuals often hold negative self-beliefs, which foster a fear of rejection and reluctance to engage in self-disclosure (Bruch, 1995).
text.formatted: Shy individuals often hold negative self-beliefs, which foster a fear of rejection and reluctance to engage in self-disclosure <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Bruch, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: This anticipatory fear of rejection may constitute a significant component of AA, contributing to social anxiety, dating anxiety, and avoidance behaviors (Hoffman & Hay, 2018).
text.formatted: This anticipatory fear of rejection may constitute a significant component of AA, contributing to social anxiety, dating anxiety, and avoidance behaviors <ref type="bibr">(Hoffman & Hay, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The literature on shyness in early-stage dating is limited, but shyness seems to constitute a crucial link in the AA model (Figure 2) that connects deficits in interpersonal communication skills with personality traits.

Note: This figure provides an overview of potential mechanisms (interactions effects on approach behaviour) underlying approach anxiety (AA), in initial encounters.
Dashed lines mark indirect effects, full lines a direct effect.
AA is at the center of the MCIF model and influenced by interpersonal performance (IP) in the left box, including hetero and homosocial competence.
On the right, multiple factors relating to anxiety, fear, phobia and attachment can show a direct or indirect effect on AA.
Shyness has a special function as it potentially mediates IP or has direct influence.
The new MCIF-AA captures the idea that AA operates across levels: biological, psychological, and social.
A central question is whether AA constitutes a valid psychological construct, and if male reluctance to approach women is evolutionarily rooted or socially conditioned.
Evolutionary psychologists tend to argue that sex differences in initiation strategies reflect adaptive reproductive pressures (e.g., Buss & Schmitt, 1993 , 2016; Larsen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Evolutionary psychologists tend to argue that sex differences in initiation strategies reflect adaptive reproductive pressures (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Buss & Schmitt, 1993</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Larsen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Men tend to adopt direct approaches to attract mates, with higher social status linked to reproductive success via reduced childlessness (Zhang & Santtila, 2022).
text.formatted: Men tend to adopt direct approaches to attract mates, with higher social status linked to reproductive success via reduced childlessness <ref type="bibr" target="#b209">(Zhang & Santtila, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Women, by contrast, are thought to favor indirect tactics (e.g., mediated introductions or passive signaling) and emphasize traits like youth and health to appeal to male preferences.
Female mate selection is shaped by evolved priorities such as resource acquisition, warmth, and trustworthiness (Simpson & Gangestad, 1991 , 1992; Sprecher et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Female mate selection is shaped by evolved priorities such as resource acquisition, warmth, and trustworthiness <ref type="bibr">(Simpson & Gangestad, 1991</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b177">Sprecher et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Men may thus experience elevated anxiety when perceiving deficiencies in these valued domains, reinforcing sensitivity to rejection cues.

Many theorists hypothesized (H1) that AA in men is influenced by evolutionary pressures stemming from female mate selectivity, which increases men's uncertainty about the success of their courtship attempts (e.g., especially in lay conversations, see Bachaud et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Many theorists hypothesized (H1) that AA in men is influenced by evolutionary pressures stemming from female mate selectivity, which increases men's uncertainty about the success of their courtship attempts (e.g., especially in lay conversations, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bachaud et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: AA presents a paradox when viewed through the lens of strategic pluralism theory (Trivers, 1972; Gangestad & Simpson, 2000), which posits that men are generally inclined to maximize reproductive success through multiple partners, while women's preferences vary by relational context.
text.formatted: AA presents a paradox when viewed through the lens of strategic pluralism theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b192">(Trivers, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Gangestad & Simpson, 2000)</ref>, which posits that men are generally inclined to maximize reproductive success through multiple partners, while women's preferences vary by relational context.

text.text: The inhibitory nature of AA, which reduces men's likelihood of initiating romantic interactions, appears to contradict this evolutionary framework, prompting critical questions about its origins and adaptive function.
One important insight may stem from sex differences in dating goals.
While both men and women seek to reduce uncertainty and assess romantic potential, men more frequently report sexual motives that may be less tied to romantic interest (Mongeau, 2004).
text.formatted: While both men and women seek to reduce uncertainty and assess romantic potential, men more frequently report sexual motives that may be less tied to romantic interest <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Mongeau, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: However, both sexes prioritize physical attractiveness in short-term contexts and pursue long-term partnerships (Li & Kenrick, 2006; Wiederman & Dubois, 1998; Sprecher et al., 2008).
text.formatted: However, both sexes prioritize physical attractiveness in short-term contexts and pursue long-term partnerships <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Li & Kenrick, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b204">Wiederman & Dubois, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b177">Sprecher et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These findings highlight that not all individuals align with stereotypical mating goals.
AA may thus reflect a learned sense of mismatch between personal intentions and perceived dating norms, contributing to uncertainty and inhibition in romantic initiation.
A second hypothesis (H2) may thus hold that AA stems from a perceived mismatch between personal dating goals and societal or partner expectations, leading to uncertainty and fear of rejection.

Men exhibit greater variance in reproductive success than women, with some men fathering disproportionately more offspring, but female reproductive success is more evenly distributed (Buss et al., 2016; Favre & Sornette, 2012; Ross et al., 2023); also genetic studies indicate that fewer men contributed to current human generations (Favre et al., 2012; Karmin et al., 2015; Lippold et al., 2014).

text.text: This higher variance in male reproductive success is largely driven by sexual selection, wherein women tend to prefer mates with greater status and resources, prompting male-male competition and risk-taking behaviors, often linked to higher male mortality rates (Buss et al., 2016; Larsen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This higher variance in male reproductive success is largely driven by sexual selection, wherein women tend to prefer mates with greater status and resources, prompting male-male competition and risk-taking behaviors, often linked to higher male mortality rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Buss et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Larsen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While human monogamy moderates reproductive skew compared to the polygynous patterns typical in other mammals, disparities remain (Ross et al., 2023).
text.formatted: While human monogamy moderates reproductive skew compared to the polygynous patterns typical in other mammals, disparities remain <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">(Ross et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A plausible hypothesis is that AA functions as an adaptive regulatory mechanism, fostering caution in contexts with high perceived rejection risk, thereby reducing wasted mating effort and social costs in ancestral environments (Gilbert, 2001).
text.formatted: A plausible hypothesis is that AA functions as an adaptive regulatory mechanism, fostering caution in contexts with high perceived rejection risk, thereby reducing wasted mating effort and social costs in ancestral environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Gilbert, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: A third hypothesis (H3) is therefore that AA in men evolved as an adaptive response to the high variance in male reproductive success, serving to optimize the timing and context of courtship to increase the likelihood of mate acceptance.
AA may be especially salient during emerging adulthood (ages 18-29), a developmental stage marked by the pursuit of intimacy, romantic exploration, and identity formation (Davila et al., 2020).
text.formatted: AA may be especially salient during emerging adulthood (ages 18-29), a developmental stage marked by the pursuit of intimacy, romantic exploration, and identity formation <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Davila et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The emotional significance of relationship choices during this period may heighten sensitivity to rejection.
Age and life experience are key moderating factors; as individuals gain relational experience, self-confidence and social competence typically increase, potentially reducing AA.
Conversely, limited experience or underdeveloped social skills-common in high-pressure environments like college-may sustain or exacerbate AA during this critical life stage.
A fourth hypothesis (H4) is therefore that emerging adults with less relationship experience will exhibit higher levels of AA compared to their more experienced peers.
This effect will be more pronounced in high-pressure social environments (H4b), such as college settings, where dating and relationship exploration are more prevalent.

While the tendency to AA might be rooted in evolutionary theories, social learning might also have a strong influence on behaviour and perceptions. Howard et al. (1987) acknowledge the impact of sex role socialisation and power dynamics. Sadalla et al. (1987) also recognise the role of traditional sex difference in heterosexual attraction.

text.text: This acknowledgement opens the door for social learning to shape anxieties and fears related to social interaction, including approaching women (e.g., Hoffman & Hay, 2018).
text.formatted: This acknowledgement opens the door for social learning to shape anxieties and fears related to social interaction, including approaching women (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Hoffman & Hay, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We could therefore hypothesize (H5) that men who report higher levels of reluctance to approach women will show greater physiological stress responses during social interactions, supporting an innate basis for this behavior.
However, some behaviors may have an innate component that is then refined through social learning.

Evolutionary agent-based simulations have demonstrated that genetic preparedness (an evolutionary adaptation) and social learning often co-evolve in dangerous environments, providing complementary benefits (Lindström et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Evolutionary agent-based simulations have demonstrated that genetic preparedness (an evolutionary adaptation) and social learning often co-evolve in dangerous environments, providing complementary benefits <ref type="bibr">(Lindström et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: It is possible that AA arises from a combination of innate predispositions and learned behaviors, requiring an explanation that integrates both aspects.
Another potential contributor to the development of AA in men may lie in ingroup-outgroup dynamics, as outlined by Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1979).
text.formatted: Another potential contributor to the development of AA in men may lie in ingroup-outgroup dynamics, as outlined by Social Identity Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b188">(Tajfel & Turner, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: This framework posits that individuals classify others into ingroups and outgroups based on salient identity markers such as sex, race, or social roles, often leading to ingroup favoritism and outgroup avoidance or distrust.

Men may perceive the ingroup (i.e., other men) as familiar and non-threatening due to shared experiences and social norms, whereas women, as outgroup members, may be viewed as unfamiliar or even threatening due to biological, cultural, or social differences.

Evolutionary psychologists suggest that such avoidance of outgroup members may have served an adaptive function in ancestral environments by reducing risks of harm, competition, or social instability (Van Vugt & Schaller, 2008).
text.formatted: Evolutionary psychologists suggest that such avoidance of outgroup members may have served an adaptive function in ancestral environments by reducing risks of harm, competition, or social instability <ref type="bibr" target="#b197">(Van Vugt & Schaller, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Men's avoidance of women may also be rooted in evolutionary strategies linked to male-male competition and coalition maintenance.
Dominant individuals-particularly males-have historically been perceived as threats by outgroup members due to risks of aggression or resource loss (Tooby & Cosmides, 2010).

The primary finding of this paper is the notable scarcity of academic literature on AA.

This gap may stem from the topic's interdisciplinary complexity-spanning psychological, sociological, and cultural domains-as well as limited scholarly recognition of male-specific barriers in initiating romantic interactions.

Additionally, the predominance of female researchers in dating-related studies raises the possibility that research priorities may reflect sex-based differences in perspective, potentially shaping the field's focus.
Much of the literature in this domain spans multiple decades and relies heavily on self-report measures, self-assessments, or controlled laboratory studies.
Given individuals' limited introspective accuracy in romantic contexts, the validity of such data is questionable.
These methodological limitations underscore the need for more ecologically valid and methodologically rigorous approaches in future research.

This paper was initially conceived as a comprehensive literature review on the topic of "approach anxiety".
However, a significant gap in the existing literature was uncovered.
As a result, the thesis pivoted towards providing a broad overview of dating research, while also proposing potential theoretical frameworks for future investigations.
Based on the current knowledge summarized in this thesis, there is substantial evidence pointing toward AA as a genuine phenomenon affecting many men.
However, only precise and targeted research can uncover the definitive answer to this intriguing question.
This question presents substantial research challenges, particularly when considering the influence of various factors such as culture, religion, and societal norms.

Despite these challenges, this thesis serves as an important first step in a burgeoning research area with vast potential to contribute to the understanding of men's social and relational behaviors, and ultimately, to the development of effective interventions.

These findings suggest that the SHI is an effective tool for identifying individuals who may face challenges in heterosexual social interactions.

The SIAS evaluates broader social discomfort, such as fear of embarrassment or rejection, making it particularly useful for studying individuals with social anxiety disorder.
Scores on this scale range from 10 to 40, with higher scores indicating greater self-esteem.
The SIAS exhibits excellent reliability, with Cronbach's alpha values ranging from 0.88 to 0.94, and a test-retest reliability of approximately 0.86 over several months.
Additionally, its strong correlations with other established measures of social anxiety underscore its validity as a diagnostic and research tool.

text.text: Taking together, all 3 theories together might help to develop a fundamental theory to understand AA.
A future theory might propose that men's behavior in initial encounters is driven by adaptive strategies to mitigate perceived risks and maximize relational rewards.
Drawing from social penetration theory men likely engage in shallow, low-risk disclosures to test compatibility while avoiding vulnerability.

The intimacy process model provides the concept of responsiveness, which highlights the importance of feedback; positive signals from a potential partner can alleviate AA and encourage further interaction, while negative or neutral responses may inhibit engagement.

Stimulus-value-role theory contributes to understanding AA by framing how men evaluate potential partners across stages, focusing first on surfacelevel stimuli (e.g., appearance or social cues), then exploring shared values, and only later considering long-term role alignment.
This integrated framework could further explore how external influences, such as sex difference and prior experiences, shape men's approach strategies.
For instance, societal expectations may pressure men to initiate contact, amplifying anxiety, while responsiveness from a partner may serve as a critical factor in overcoming this barrier.
Similarly, cultural and individual factors, such as attachment styles or previous relationship successes, might influence the degree of risk men are willing to take.
By combining these theories, a future model could offer a dynamic, context-sensitive understanding of male behavior in romantic initiation.

This framework would not only highlight the complexity of earlystage interactions but also suggest interventions-such as social skills training or re-framing societal norms-to support men navigating these pivotal moments in forming connections.

Research on relationship initiation has been informed by several theoretical frameworks, each offering unique insights into how romantic connections are formed (Clark et al., 2099).
text.formatted: Research on relationship initiation has been informed by several theoretical frameworks, each offering unique insights into how romantic connections are formed <ref type="bibr">(Clark et al., 2099)</ref>.

text.text: These theories explore different aspects of attraction, compatibility, and the processes underlying relationship development.
However, critics argue that these theories remain incomplete, often failing to fully encapsulate the complexities of relationship initiation.
Altman and Taylor's (1973) Social Penetration Theory highlights the critical role of self-disclosure in relationship initiation.
This theory posits that relationships deepen as individuals gradually share more personal information, both in breadth (variety of topics) and depth (intimacy of topics).
Early stages of relationship development involve rapid disclosure, but the rate slows as the relationship matures.
Reciprocity, where both partners equally share personal information, is essential for the progression of intimacy.
The theory underscores self-disclosure as a mechanism for building trust and connection in early interactions.
Reis and Shaver (1988) conceptualized intimacy as a dynamic, reciprocal process involving selfdisclosure and partner responsiveness.
Their model suggests that the initiation of intimacy depends on the ability of a partner to listen empathetically, demonstrate understanding, and respond with care and acceptance.
Such responses encourage further disclosure, creating a positive feedback loop that fosters intimacy and relationship growth.
The model also introduces the concept of "interpretive filters,"
acknowledging that individuals' perceptions of their partner's actions influence the development of intimacy.
Proposed by Murstein (1970), the Stimulus-Value-Role (SVR) theory conceptualizes romantic relationship development as a staged process.
text.formatted: Proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Murstein (1970)</ref>, the Stimulus-Value-Role (SVR) theory conceptualizes romantic relationship development as a staged process.

text.text: In the initial stimulus stage, attraction is largely based on superficial characteristics, such as physical appearance or initial impressions.
As the relationship progresses, shared values, beliefs, and attitudes (the value stage) become more influential.
Ultimately, long-term compatibility depends on the roles each partner assumes (the role stage), such as those related to career, family, or household dynamics.

This theory underscores how relationships evolve from surfacelevel attraction to deeper emotional and functional compatibility. Levinger and Snoek's (1972) ABCDE Model provides a sequential framework for understanding relationship progression.
text.formatted: This theory underscores how relationships evolve from surfacelevel attraction to deeper emotional and functional compatibility. <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Levinger and Snoek's (1972)</ref> ABCDE Model provides a sequential framework for understanding relationship progression.

text.text: The model outlines five stages:
Attraction: Initial impressions, influenced by appearance, behavior, and nonverbal cues.
Building: Exploration of shared personality traits, values, and interests to foster connection.
Continuation: Strengthening the relationship through trust, affection, and commitment.
Deterioration and Ending: While part of the model, these latter stages are not central to the initiation of relationships.
The ABCDE Model emphasizes the early importance of physical and emotional commonalities in building connections, with later stages focusing on relationship maintenance and breakdown.

text.text: Satisfaction:
The balance of rewards and costs in the relationship.
Investments: Time, effort, and resources that would be lost if the relationship ended.
Alternatives:
The perceived quality of other potential partners.
Norms: Social and personal expectations about staying in a relationship.
The theory emphasizes that early relationship development is influenced by the interplay of these factors, shaping decisions to pursue or deepen romantic connections.

The evident absence of "approach anxiety" from academic literature opens a critical opportunity for scholarly investigation if such a construct really existed.

Establishing the validity and scope of this construct is imperative, as it may shed light on the liability of the mainstream literature and an undiscovered clinical aspect for potentially suffering men.
To initiate research into a potential fear in men, it is essential to first establish and understand relevant theoretical principles.
A critical consideration is the context of this "fear", as it inherently involves the interaction of two individuals.

As a dyad, the effects can be partitioned into three components: those attributable to the perceiver (P), those associated with the observed target (T), and the emergent effects resulting from the unique interaction between P and T.

Historically, researchers and theorists have acknowledged that attraction is influenced by both internal processes within the perceiver-such as motivation, comparison levels, and personality-and external characteristics of the target, such as physical attractiveness (summarized in Sprecher et al., 2008).
